opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be back.

I think a lot of the confusion in timelines debates comes from people forecasting different things without realising it. You'll hear one person say "AGI by 2030" and another say "not for decades," and often they're not really disagreeing about the world. They're disagreeing about what the target is.

So the first thing I'd say is that we should be predicting things that matter for decisions, rather than a label like "AGI," which means very different things to different people. For some it's a system that can pass as human in conversation. For others it's something that can do every economically valuable task better than any person. Those could be many years apart.

What I care about most are the transitions where the world changes in a way that matters for risk and for what we should do now. A few candidates:

One is when AI systems can substantially automate AI research itself. That's crucial because it could compress progress dramatically. If the systems are doing the work that drives their own improvement, timelines for everything downstream might shorten a lot.

Another is when AI can do most remote, computer-based work at a level that transforms the economy. That's a clearer economic threshold, and it would bring enormous changes to labour markets, to power, and to which actors have leverage.

A third is when systems become capable enough that losing control of them would be catastrophic, for example if they could act autonomously over long periods, acquire resources, or evade oversight. From a safety point of view, that's arguably the date we most need to know, because it tells us how much time we have to get alignment and governance right.

I'd also want forecasters to give full probability distributions rather than single dates. The median isn't what matters most for planning around risk. If there's even a 10 or 15 percent chance that transformative systems arrive within a few years, that should heavily shape what we do now, even if the median is later. The left tail is where a lot of the action is.

Finally, it's worth being honest about how much our forecasts depend on assumptions about scaling. Recently there have been signs that the old recipe of pre-training on ever more data with ever more compute is giving diminishing returns. Much of the progress has shifted to things like reinforcement learning and using more compute at inference time, which have quite different cost profiles. So a good forecast shouldn't just extrapolate a curve. It should be explicit about which drivers of progress it's assuming will continue, and how quickly they might run into limits.

In short, forecast the capabilities that change the strategic picture, give the whole distribution, and show your working on the underlying assumptions. That makes the forecasts far more useful, and far easier to argue about productively.

r001.rationale: The response proposes forecasting decision-relevant capability milestones and risk distributions, but does not identify actual availability as the key forecast or distinguish it from hypothetical capability under danger-disregarding optimal behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that a lot of the disagreement about "AI timelines" is really a disagreement about what question is being asked, and we'd make a lot more progress if people were explicit about it.

The classic framing was something like "when will we get human-level AI?" But that phrase has become almost useless, because capabilities aren't arriving as a single bundle. Systems already exceed humans at some things and lag badly at others, and that unevenness isn't going away. So a forecast that says "2029" without saying 2029 for what is hard to evaluate and hard to act on.

So I'd push forecasters towards predicting things that are, first, operationalised, and second, decision-relevant. On the first point: you want milestones with a clear resolution criterion, like a system that can do a particular class of economically valuable work end to end, or that can carry out a research project of a certain length without human intervention, or that meets a specific threshold on a benchmark we've agreed in advance is meaningful. The METR-style "task horizon" work is a good example of the kind of thing I mean, where you can actually track a quantity over time and see whether the trend is holding.

On the second point, the milestone that I think matters most is the one that changes the dynamics of the situation. The really important transition is when AI systems can substantially automate AI research and development itself. That's the point where you could get a feedback loop, where progress stops being bottlenecked on the number of human researchers, and things could go much faster than the trends that preceded it would suggest. If I could only have one forecast, it would be the probability distribution over that date, because that's what determines how much time we have to get governance, alignment and institutions in order.

And I'd add a third thing: forecasts should be distributions, not point estimates, and people should be explicit about the drivers. If your timeline depends on compute continuing to scale at the current rate, say so, and say what you'd update on if investment slowed or if the algorithmic efficiency gains dried up. Then when the world moves, we can actually tell whose model was right rather than just arguing about vibes.

What I'd like to get away from is the pattern where "timelines" becomes a kind of tribal marker, where saying a short number signals you're a serious person in one community and a long number signals it in another. The reason to forecast is that the answer changes what we should do, and a good forecast is one that someone could actually use.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes forecasting when AI can substantially automate AI research and development, but it does not distinguish when advanced AI will actually become available from when it could under hypothetical danger-disregarding conditions.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to be clearer about what event we’re trying to forecast. People often ask when we’ll get AGI, but they can mean quite different things by that. Do they mean a system that can do every task a human can do? One that can do most economically valuable work? Or one that could radically accelerate scientific and technological progress? Those might happen at quite different times.

For thinking about existential risk, I’m particularly interested in when AI could become capable of taking control away from humanity. That doesn’t necessarily require it to match every human ability. A system could have weaknesses in some areas and still be overwhelmingly powerful in the areas that matter.

And I’d distinguish that from the point at which AI can substantially accelerate AI research itself. That could tell us something about how much time we have between reaching an important capability threshold and reaching something much more powerful.

So I’d like forecasts of several clearly specified milestones, with uncertainty around each, rather than a single date for ‘AGI’. The question is which developments would change our situation, and how much warning we’d have.

r001.rationale: The response asks for forecasts of specified capability milestones, including taking control and accelerating AI research. It does not identify when advanced AI systems will actually become available, or contrast that with hypothetical capability under danger-disregarding behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to be clearer about what the endpoint is. There are several different things people might mean by advanced AI, and forecasts of them can come apart quite substantially. You might mean a system that can do most of the tasks a human can do, or one that can automate most economically valuable work, or one that could pose an existential risk. Those aren’t obviously the same milestone.

For the purposes of thinking about existential risk, I’m most interested in when we might develop systems that could gain power over humanity, such that our future is no longer under our control. But that’s quite a difficult thing to turn into a precise forecasting question. So there’s a role for forecasting more concrete capabilities along the way. We just need to be careful that we don’t answer a question about performance on some collection of tasks and then treat it as though we’ve answered the question about when humanity could lose control.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes possible AI milestones and focuses on when systems could threaten human control, but it does not say forecasts should target when advanced AI will actually become available rather than when it could be built under hypothetical optimal behavior that ignores danger.
